paper_title: When Morphs Look Better: Face Image Quality as a Training-Free Signal for Morphing Attack Detection

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Face image quality assessment (FIQA) estimates the utility of a face image for automated face recognition and has been proposed as a morphing attack detection (MAD) signal that requires no morph-specific training. We evaluate 17 FIQA methods from all current FIQA categories on 20 morphing attack sets from two datasets, FRLL and FEI, including five diffusion-based attack sets. Each quality score is used directly as a MAD decision score. Unlike prior work, which inverted a quality measure when this lowered its error, we fix the score direction of each method in advance from its definition, so that cases in which morphs receive higher quality than bona fide samples remain visible. On FRLL, DifFIQA(R) achieves a mean D-EER of 11.42%, and together with CLIB-FIQA and eDifFIQA(L) clearly outperforms all other FIQA methods. A strong separation of bona fide and morph scores does not imply good detection performance: on the diffusion-based attacks, up to 11 of 17 methods assign higher quality to morphs than to bona fide samples, and the largest reversed separation in the study coincides with the worst detection result of the study. Performance also depends strongly on the attack: GraFIQs(L), the best detector of DCMorph and Arc2Morph on FRLL, performs poorly on the landmark-based and GAN-based attacks. On FEI, the lowest mean D-EER is 39.75%, and a threshold set on the bona fide data of one dataset does not transfer to the other.

sections.title: Morphing Attack Detection
sections.content: I. INTRODUCTION Face recognition (FR) is widely used for identity verification in travel documents and border control. face morphing attack combines the face images of two or more subjects into one image that can be verified against each of them [1], so that document issued to one person can be used by another. Morphs can also be difficult for human examiners to detect [2], [3], which makes morphing attack detection (MAD) necessary part of secure FR systems. Single-image MAD is mostly addressed as supervised binary classification, from handcrafted descriptors to deep representations [4]. The performance of such detectors depends on their training data and degrades when the morphing technique, the image source, or the post-processing differs at deployment [5]. As morph generation has moved from landmark-based blending through GAN-based interpolation to identity-conditioned diffusion [3], Hao Peng, Fu Bo, and Mahmoud Elshirbeny contributed equally to this work. detectors trained on known attacks are regularly confronted with new attack types. This motivates detection signals that are not learned from morphs. Face image quality assessment (FIQA) estimates the utility of face image for recognition [6] and is trained without morphs. Since morphing alters texture, geometry, and identity information, it can shift the FIQA score. In that case, the score can be thresholded directly as MAD score, without morph data or training, as only the threshold is set on bona fide images. Fu and Damer studied this with five FIQA and five general image quality measures on five morphing datasets [7]. Since then, newer FIQA methods have been proposed in all categories, including methods based on the robustness to diffusion-based perturbation and methods that probe pretrained FR model through gradients, intermediate layers, attention, or pruning, and diffusion-based morphing synthesizes the morph instead of blending two photographs. To our knowledge, quality-based MAD has not been evaluated with these FIQA methods or on diffusion-based attacks. We evaluate 17 FIQA methods from all categories, without retraining, on 20 morphing attack sets from two bona fide datasets, covering landmark-based, GAN-based, and diffusion-based morphing. Each FIQA score has defined direction, and prior work inverted quality measure when this lowered its average error over the attacks [7]. This choice can present method that assigns higher quality to morphs than to bona fide samples as successful detector, and it requires knowledge of the attack. We instead fix the score direction of each method in advance and never change it per attack. Our contributions are threefold. (i) We evaluate 17 FIQA methods from all categories as training-free single-image MAD scores under one protocol and operating point, including five diffusion-based attack sets. (ii) We use protocol with fixed score direction and signed separation measure, which shows that strong separation of bona fide and morph scores does not imply good detection performance, most clearly on diffusion-based attacks. (iii) We analyze the limits of the approach: the FIQA performance of method does not reliably predict its MAD performance, detection performance differs strongly between datasets, and threshold set on bona fide data does not transfer between them. II. RELATED WORK A. Face Image Quality Assessment FIQA estimates the utility of face image for recognition rather than its perceived visual quality [6]. Following [8], we group FIQA methods into four categories. Supervised methods regress quality label: FaceQnet uses labels derived from ICAO compliance [9], SDD-FIQA the distance between genuine and impostor similarity distributions [10], and CLIBFIQA quality anchors calibrated against facial attributes [11]. Unsupervised methods require no quality labels and form two categories. In non-FR-model methods, quality comes from perturbing the input image with an external generative model rather than from the internals of the FR model: DifFIQA measures the resulting change of FR embeddings and distills it into regression model, DifFIQA(R) [12], and eDifFIQA improves this distillation [13]. FR-probing methods derive quality from the internals of frozen FR model, using the stability of embeddings under dropout (SER-FIQ [14]), gradient magnitudes (GraFIQs [15]), the stability of embeddings across ViT blocks (ViTNT-FIQA [16]), informative intermediate layers (FROQ [17]), the change of embeddings under pruning (PreFIQs [8]), or pre-softmax self-attention (ATTNFIQA [18]). Self-supervised methods derive quality from the FR training objective, either jointly with recognition or with an additional head on the FR model: MagFace through the embedding magnitude [19], PFE through an uncertainty head on frozen FR model [20], ViT-FIQA through learnable quality token [21], CR-FIQA through relative classifiability [22], CARPM-FIQA through relative point margins accumulated over training [23], and EX-FIQA through early exits of ViT-FIQA [24]. These methods were developed and evaluated on bona fide face images, and none was designed for morphs, so whether and in which direction method responds to morphing has to be measured. We include methods from all four categories and examine whether FIQA performance predicts MAD performance. B. Morphing Attacks and Their Detection landmarks in both images, Morph generation operates either on the image level or on learned representation [3]. We cover both with 20 attack sets: on FRLL, the five techniques of MAD22 [25] and three diffusion-based techniques [3], [26], [27], and the twelve techniques of FEI-Morph V3 [28]. Image-level methods interpolate them, detect facial and blend the texture: OpenCV uses 68 landmarks, Delaunay triangulation, and alpha blending [29]. FaceMorpher is also landmark-based, but the version used in MAD22 is commercial off-the-shelf tool whose technical details are not released [25]. WebMorph uses 189 landmarks annotated for the underlying dataset, which reduces artifacts [30]. Such morphs typically contain blending artifacts and geometric inconsistencies [2]. Representation-level methods interpolate in learned latent space: MIPGAN-I and MIPGAN-II optimize perceptual quality, identity, identity difference, and structural objectives with StyleGAN and StyleGAN2, respectively, and produce high-resolution morphs with few visible artifacts [2]. DCMorph is diffusion-based and injects identity features of both subjects into the denoising process via decoupled crossattention, while DDIM inversion with spherical interpolation provides the initial latent [3]. MorDIFF interpolates the semantic latent of diffusion autoencoder [26], and Arc2Morph interpolates the identity embeddings that condition the face generator Arc2Face [27]. LADIMO [31] and StableMorph [32] use latent diffusion and Stable Diffusion, respectively, and landmark-based morphing has been further improved as well [33]. Unlike landmark-based morphs, diffusion-based morphs are synthesized from an interpolated conditioning signal rather than blended from two photographs. MAD is performed either differentially, using trusted live capture, or on the suspected image alone, which is our setting. Both are surveyed in [4]. Single-image MAD is mostly addressed as supervised binary classification, from handcrafted texture and forensic descriptors to deep networks trained with morph labels [4]. Its main challenge is generalization, since detection cues depend the source data, compression, on the morphing algorithm, and re-digitization, and degrade when these are not seen in training [5]. Proposed solutions extend the training data, treat morphs as anomalies without using morph labels [34], or adapt foundation models, such as MADation [35] and the selfsupervised SelfMAD++ [36], but all of them train model. In quality-based MAD, no model is trained, and the score of pretrained FIQA method is used directly. Fu et al. showed that morphing shifts the quality distributions of morph images away from those of bona fide images [37], and Fu and Damer evaluated this for MAD on five morphing datasets with ten quality measures [7]. In differential MAD, quality has been used to support separately trained detector rather than as the decision score [38], [39]. SYN-MAD 2022 released the MAD22 benchmark and ranked submissions by the attack error at fixed bona fide error of 20% [25], i.e. MACER at BSCER = 20% in the terms of ISO/IEC 20059 [40]. Since all attacks share one bona fide set, fixing BSCER yields single threshold and makes the attacks comparable. We adopt this benchmark and operating point and replace the trained detector with pretrained FIQA score. Our work differs from prior quality-based MAD [7] in two ways: it evaluated five FIQA methods, none of them from the non-FR-model category or among the recent FR-probing methods, whereas we evaluate 17 methods from all four categories, and it inverted quality measure when this lowered its average EER over the attacks, whereas we fix the score direction in advance. In addition, quality-based MAD has, to our knowledge, only been evaluated on landmark-based and GAN-based attacks [7], [37], while we include five diffusion-based attack sets. III. METHODOLOGY Each FIQA method is pretrained function that maps an image to scalar score, and we evaluate whether this score alone separates bona fide from morph images. Let sm(x) be the output of method for image x. The detector classifies as an attack if qm(x) τm, where qm is the directionnormalized score defined below. We consider the approach training-free if (i) the FIQA model is released model trained for recognition utility and never exposed to morphs, (ii) no MAD classifier is trained and no method selection uses attack data, and (iii) no detector parameter, neither the score direction πm nor the threshold τm, is derived from attacks. Attack labels are used only to measure performance. Condition (iii) distinguishes this protocol from prior work, which inverted quality measure when this lowered its average EER over the attacks [7]. FIQA methods differ in score direction: most scores increase with utility, while some increase with degradation, such as embedding uncertainty or gradient magnitude. Before any MAD evaluation, each method is therefore assigned fixed πm {+1, 1} according to the meaning of its score in the original publication, and all analyses use qm(x) = πmsm(x), so that larger qm always means higher predicted utility. πm is set per method and never changed per attack. Selecting the direction that minimizes the error, per method [7] or per method and attack, lowers the reported error but requires knowledge of the attack and violates (iii). With fixed direction, an error above 50% occurs when morphing shifts the score opposite to its meaning. We use the metrics of ISO/IEC 20059 [40]: the morphing attack classification error rate (MACER) is the proportion of morphs classified as bona fide, and the bona fide sample classification error rate (BSCER) is the proportion of bona fide samples classified as morphs. As thresholdindependent measure, we report the detection equal error rate (D-EER), read at the ROC point closest to MACER = BSCER, between the bona fide set and each attack set. Since the D-EER threshold is determined from both distributions, we also use threshold that can be set in practice. τm is the lowest bona fide score at which BSCER reaches 20% (41/204 = 20.10% on FRLL, 40/200 = 20% on FEI). It is applied unchanged to all attacks of the same dataset, and we report the resulting MACER. This is the operating point of SYN-MAD 2022 [25], where the threshold is set on the bona fide images of the evaluated dataset. All metrics are computed per attack, and the mean D-EER and mean MACER over the attacks of dataset summarize each method. We report 95% confidence intervals of the mean D-EER from 1,000 bootstrap replicates. Each replicate draws identities with replacement, weights each bona fide image by the number of draws of its identity and each morph by the product of the draws of its two identities, so that morphs with an undrawn identity are excluded, and recomputes the D-EER of every attack and their mean. MAD22 contains 204 frontal bona fide images of 102 subjects from the Face Research Lab London (FRLL) dataset and 1,000 morphing pairs, selected as the 250 most similar pairs by ElasticFace-Arc cosine similarity per gender and expression [25]. The number of attacks differs per technique: 16 OpenCV morphs with mouth-region artifacts were removed, WebMorph was applied only to neutral images since it failed on smiling faces, and landmark detection failed on one MIPGAN-II morph [25]. The second dataset is FEI-Morph V3 [28], based on the FEI face database [41]: 200 frontal bona fide images of 200 subjects and twelve morphing techniques, eight landmarkbased or commercial [33], [42][44] and four generative. Two of the generative ones are diffusion-based, namely Arc2Morph and StableMorph [32], and two are described only as inspired by LADIMO [31] and by the StyleGAN2-based demorphing method StyleDemorpher [45]. The providers do not document how these two sets produce morphs, and the LADIMOinspired set contains 999 morphs. The FEI FaceMorpher and Arc2Morph sets may differ in implementation or settings from their FRLL counterparts, and SYN-MAD 2022 describes the MAD22 FaceMorpher as commercial off-the-shelf tool. Within each dataset, all attack sets are evaluated against the same bona fide images, so that one threshold derived from bona fide data applies to all its attacks. Faces are detected and aligned to 112 112 pixels with MTCNN [46]. Further preprocessing follows each released implementation. No morph-specific preprocessing or attack-dependent tuning is applied. We evaluate the 17 methods in Tab. I, which cover all four categories of Sec. II-A. Each is released model with its original weights and is neither retrained nor calibrated on morphing data. Tab. also lists πm: fourteen scores increase with predicted utility and are used unchanged, and three measure degradation-related quantity and are inverted, namely PFE (embedding uncertainty [20]), GraFIQs (a gradient magnitude that increases as sample deviates from the training distribution [15]), and PreFIQs (the change of embeddings under pruning [8]). SER-FIQ is stochastic, as its scores are computed from repeated dropout passes, so its results carry sampling variance. MagFace and CR-FIQA(L) are min-max normalized with constants from an external dataset. This affine transform changes neither nor the error rates. The suffixes denote the evaluated variants: DifFIQA(R) is the regression model distilled from DifFIQA, eDifFIQA(L) the variant with the large backbone, GraFIQs(L), CR-FIQA(L), and CARPM-FIQA(L) use iResNet-100 backbones trained on MS1MV2, ViT-FIQA(T) is the quality-token variant, and EXFIQA-FW(T) fuses all twelve early exits of ViT-FIQA(T) with depth-dependent weights. The FR-probing methods use the FR models released with them: an ArcFace ResNet-100 for SERFIQ, GraFIQs(L), and PreFIQs, an AdaFace IR-101 for FROQ, and AdaFace ViT-B and ViT-S models trained on WebFace4M for ViTNT-FIQA and ATTN-FIQA, respectively. Detection Performance of FIQA Scores Tab. III also reports the D-EER per attack and, per method, the mean D-EER and the mean MACER at the fixed operating point. On FRLL, DifFIQA(R) achieves the best results with mean D-EER of 11.42% (confidence interval [9.0, 14.0], below the mean of every other method) and mean MACER of 10.75%, followed by CLIB-FIQA and eDifFIQA(L) with 16.99/20.03% and 24.34/30.47% (mean DEER/mean MACER), while the fourth-ranked method by both mean D-EER and mean MACER, GraFIQs(L), reaches mean MACER of 55.66%. Quality-based MAD is thus effective on this dataset without morph data or training, with the threshold set on its bona fide images. Identifying DifFIQA(R) as the best method, however, uses the attack labels of this evaluation, and how deployer could select method without attack data remains open. Performance depends strongly on the attack. All three reach their lowest D-EER on FaceMorpher (0.003.40%) and their highest on DCMorph (30.00-63.20%), and eDifFIQA(L) is also close to chance on Arc2Morph (49.39%). PFE, ViT-FIQA(T), and FROQ reach DCMorph D-EERs of 75.30%, 78.40%, and 94.90%, well above 50% and consistent with their negative in Tab. III. B. Transfer Across Datasets Detection performance differs strongly between FRLL and FEI (Tab. IV). Separation is weak, with not exceeding 1.03 on any landmark-based FEI set. The lowest mean DEER is 39.75% and the lowest mean MACER 58.96%, both achieved by ViT-FIQA(T), whose D-EER confidence interval [37.3, 42.6] includes the means of the next four methods (MagFace, EX-FIQA-FW(T), eDifFIQA(L), and PFE), while DifFIQA(R), the best method on FRLL, reaches mean DEER of 44.25%. As the attack sets differ, this does not isolate the effect of the bona fide data, which the following threshold experiment does. Set at BSCER = 20% on FRLL, the thresholds of DifFIQA(R) and CLIB-FIQA yield BSCER of 100% on FEI. Set on FEI, they yield BSCER of 0% on FRLL with mean MACER of 90.9% and 98.1%, respectively. For DifFIQA(R), the mean bona fide score is 0.86 on FEI and 0.93 on FRLL. The datasets differ in capture setup, image resolution, and subjects, and our experiments do not isolate the cause of the shift. The threshold is thus independent of the attacks, as required by (iii), but depends on the bona fide dataset. Limitations: the bona fide sets are small (204 and 200 images), as reflected in the confidence intervals. The operating point of BSCER = 20% follows SYN-MAD 2022 [25] to allow comparison with that benchmark and is not intended as setting for deployed systems. The MorDIFF and Arc2Morph attacks are our reproductions with the authors code, and the FEI sets are used as provided. VI. CONCLUSION We evaluated face image quality as training-free signal for single-image MAD, using 17 FIQA methods on 20 morphing attack sets from two datasets, with the score direction of each method fixed in advance. On FRLL, the approach is effective: without morph data or training, DifFIQA(R) reaches mean D-EER of 11.42% and mean MACER of 10.75%. However, strong response to morphing does not imply good detection performance, since the shift can be opposite to the meaning of the score. On the diffusionbased attacks, up to 11 of 17 methods assign higher quality to morphs, and on DCMorph the method with the largest reversed separation is the worst detector, while another method detects this attack best. Reporting only the unsigned FDR, or selecting the direction per attack, would present such reversals as successful detection. Three further findings follow. First, the mean performance over attacks hides large differences between attacks: GraFIQs(L), the best detector of DCMorph and Arc2Morph on FRLL, performs poorly on the landmarkbased and GAN-based attacks. Second, the FIQA performance of method predicts its MAD performance only moderately and not robustly. Third, detection performance differs strongly between the datasets, with lowest mean D-EER of 39.75% on FEI, and threshold set on the bona fide data of one dataset does not transfer to the other. Future work should investigate whether threshold calibrated on held-out bona fide images of the target domain generalizes to new images of that domain, and which properties of FIQA method determine the direction of its response to morphing. Since FIQA usually precedes MAD to reject low-quality samples, trained MAD detectors could also be evaluated with and without such rejection, on the retained samples.

APPENDIX B
MACER PER ATTACK
sections.content: Tabs. III and IV report the mean MACER over the attacks of each dataset. Tabs. and VI list the MACER of each attack at the same operating point, i.e. with the threshold τm set at BSCER = 20% on the bona fide images of the dataset. At this operating point, random score yields MACER of about 80%. higher MACER means that morphs pass the threshold more often than bona fide images. This is the case for 52 of the 136 method-attack pairs on FRLL and 74 of the 204 pairs on FEI. SELECTING THE SCORE DIRECTION
sections.content: Our protocol fixes the score direction of each method in advance (Sec. III). Tab. VIII shows how the mean D-EER would change if the direction were chosen using the attack labels, either once per method, as in [7], or separately for each attack. Both choices violate condition (iii) of Sec. III and are shown only for comparison. The per-method choice inverts FROQ, ViTNT-FIQA, and ATTN-FIQA on FRLL and SER-FIQ, FROQ, and ViTNT-FIQA on FEI.
